These four criteria together guarantee that the translation is compositional (so it can be applied
to subterms), respects renaming of names, preserves observable behaviour, and does not create
observable traces. A comparison satisfying them is said to be faithful; a failure of any one
means the comparison is incomplete in that respect.


4.3  The outcomes

A translation may satisfy all four criteria (faithful), satisfy three of them (partial), or fail two
or more (unfaithful). In each case we can say what it preserves and what it discards.

1. Faithful translations preserve the full set of observable traces, including their order.
   They also preserve the success predicate: a term that succeeds in the source calculus will
    succeed in the target calculus with exactly the same observable outcome. The only thing lost
     is any extra behaviour introduced by the translation itself (e.g., additional steps or side‑effects).

2. Partial translations may fail completeness but retain soundness and observational equivalence.
   They preserve all traces that can be reproduced from a source term, while some successful terms
    in the source have no corresponding trace in the target.

3. Unfaithful translations break at least one of the criteria (usually both). In such cases,
   either many observable behaviours are lost or spurious behaviours appear. The translation then
     cannot be used to reason about the semantics of the source calculus without additional analysis.

These outcomes guide how a comparison should be interpreted: if a translation is faithful, it can
be used directly for reasoning; if it is partial, one must supplement it with manual proofs for the
missing cases; and if it is unfaithful, the comparison fails to be useful for preserving semantic
properties.


4.4  How the chapter uses these criteria

The rest of the book applies these criteria to compare various calculi (e.g., the λ‑calculus,
process algebras, and operational models of concurrency). Each comparison section states which
criteria are satisfied and which are violated, explains why those violations matter for reasoning,
and provides examples illustrating the preserved or lost behaviours. This systematic use ensures
that any conclusions drawn from the comparisons remain valid under the stated semantic criteria.
